mappings.note: Narrate your own thunderstorm experience in a paragraph. A personal-experience prompt that never returns to the text, so C-E1.2.
Completes a stated pair of failures (compass and radio dead). Retrieval, LO-1.
Asks the learner to imagine how a preacher and a psychologist would each read the story - their own reasoning about two interpretations, C-E1.2, not extraction from the text.
Compose an excerpt of a companion story from the other pilot's point of view. Creative composition with a set voice and format, C-E1.2.
Recounts the Dakota's flight from Paris to the landing. A sequence of narrated events, LO-1.
How the black aeroplane led him out is narrated; information extraction, LO-1, not an interpretation of who the pilot was.
Mood at the story's opening is an element of craft - the atmosphere the writer sets up. No LO in this frame names mood or tone, so the competency C-E1.4.
'Briefly evaluate the narrator's decision' asks for a judgement the learner must argue, so C-E1.2 rather than a comprehension outcome.
Speculates about what the narrator would feel after the story ends - the text does not settle it, so this is opinion with reasons, C-E1.2.
'As a reader, do you feel betrayed ... validate your opinion' is explicitly about the learner's own response, C-E1.2, not about what the story says.
A verdict on the narrator's character that must be defended from what the story shows - textual evidence, LO-3. The reader-response items above are the C-E1.2 ones.
Malformed row whose stem has swallowed a previous answer, but the live sub-question asks how to read 'He knows that I am lost' - an inference about what the second pilot really was, LO-2.
Part i asks why the author capitalised 'Wanted' - a deliberate stylistic device, C-E1.4; the other parts retrieve the pilot's decision from the extract, LO-1.
How he came to be lost - dead radio, spinning compass, dead instruments - is narrated; retrieval, LO-1.
What he saw after the twelve-degree turn is the next narrated event; extraction, LO-1.
Reproduces the story's description of the clouds. The answer is lifted from the text, so LO-1 rather than an analysis of the image.
Why the fear returned - the fuel running out - is about his state of mind at that moment, LO-2.
A presentation draft comparing the seagull's and the pilot's approaches, with a set opening line. Structured composition, C-E1.2.
Write the narrator's diary entry. First-person diary format and tone are what is marked - C-E1.2.
Explains what the narrator's relief at leaving the Dakota reveals about the ordeal he had just survived - his feeling, LO-2, not a retrievable fact.
Why the controller looked at him strangely has to be inferred from her side of the exchange - a minor character's reaction in context, LO-2.
'Who do you think helped him ... give reasons' invites competing interpretations the story deliberately leaves open, so opinion with reasoning, C-E1.2.
Supplies the meaning of the idiom 'black and blue'. Word and phrase meaning, C-E1.1.
Names the values that carried the narrator through the crisis - character drawn from the text, LO-2, in 100-120 words.
Recounts the whole episode inside the clouds and the escape. Narrated events, LO-1.
The darkness inside the cloud is stated in the text; retrieval, LO-1.
The lights of a big city are named in the narration; single-fact retrieval.
Choosing between 'calculated', 'impetuous' and 'unavoidable' is a judgement on the quality of the pilot's decision - character and context, LO-2, not a vocabulary test.
What the controller confirmed is stated in the closing exchange; retrieval, LO-1.
The purpose of the radio call - a bearing for the route - is narrated; retrieval, LO-1.
Authorship of 'Black Aeroplane'. Knowledge about the work itself, covered by C-E1.4 and by no LO.
A word-pair analogy (risk:risky::hazard:hazardous). It is presented as a vocabulary relationship rather than a sentence-level rule, so C-E1.1 and not the grammar competency.
Lead parts read the narrator's relief and the controller's laughter (LO-2); the last part asks which word could replace 'strangely', a vocabulary item (C-E1.1).
Authorship of 'His First Flight' - recall about the text itself, C-E1.4.
Authorship of 'Black Aeroplane' - the same kind of recall about the work, C-E1.4.
Identifies what the story is about (a young seagull) - the subject of the prose, retrieved, LO-1.
The reason for his fear is his belief that his wings were too weak - a state of mind, LO-2.
The threat to leave him to starve on the ledge is stated outright; retrieval, LO-1.
Skimming the waves and diving for fish are named in the text; extraction, LO-1.
Fill-in of 'food' from 'the sight of the food maddened him'. Retrieval, LO-1; the version asking what this suggests is the LO-2 item.
